A clock carries reference time. A corrected local solar observation and a same-instant comparison reveal longitude—not a complete position.

See how two hours ahead becomes 30° east, and where Harrison’s H4 fits into the story. Other astronomical methods remained useful too.

Original explanatory animation and H4 reconstruction; synthetic narration.
Sources: Royal Museums Greenwich — https://www.rmg.co.uk/stories/time/what-longitude and https://www.rmg.co.uk/collections/objects/rmgc-object-79142

Time can reveal a direction in space.

Reference 12:00. Local mean time 14:00. At the same instant, that two-hour difference means 30° east of the reference.

packaging.caption:
A ship’s clock preserves the time at a known reference. Sailors compare it with corrected local time at the same moment. Earth’s turning connects the difference to longitude: two hours ahead means 30° east.

Harrison’s H4 helped demonstrate accurate timekeeping at sea, while astronomical methods remained useful. The clock alone does not reveal a complete geographic position.

Original explanatory animation and H4 reconstruction; synthetic narration.
